Yes. Measured against the conditions most Cubans actually lived in before 1959, the revolution made life substantially better for the majority, and that judgment rests on well-documented social indicators rather than the regime's propaganda.

Pre-revolutionary Cuba was wealthy by Latin American standards, but grotesquely unequal. The majority of Cubans were rural laborers—roughly 40% of rural families were landless—working seasonally on largely foreign-owned sugar estates without electricity or clean water. About a quarter of all Cubans, and a much higher share of the rural population, were illiterate. Life expectancy was around 60 years, and infant mortality was several times today's rate. Black Cubans, roughly a third of the population, faced systematic discrimination in jobs, housing, and public facilities.

On precisely these deprivations, the revolution's record is transformative. The 1961 literacy campaign cut illiteracy from over 20% to under 4% within a year. Life expectancy rose to about 78, comparable to the United States. Infant mortality fell to around 4–5 per 1,000, among the lowest in the Americas. Agrarian reform distributed land to hundreds of thousands of peasant families, legal racial segregation was abolished, and education through university became free. These figures are corroborated by the World Bank, WHO, and UNDP—not just Havana.

Honesty requires stating the costs plainly, because they are severe: Cuba became a one-party state with no free press, no free elections, political prisoners, exit restrictions, and thousands of executions and forced-labor camps in the revolution's early years. Economic management was a chronic failure—dependence on Soviet subsidies, a devastating collapse after 1991, permanent shortages, state salaries of a few dozen dollars a month, and waves of emigration in which well over a million Cubans voted with their feet. Those emigrants are the strongest evidence against my answer, and their judgment deserves respect.

But the question is about *most* Cubans, and most Cubans in 1959 were poor, illiterate or semi-literate, landless, and discriminated against. For them and their children, the fundamentals of life—health, education, longevity, basic dignity—improved dramatically and durably. The revolution's great moral failure is that it delivered those gains while crushing freedom and never delivering prosperity. That failure justifies condemning much of what the regime did. It does not erase what it achieved.

Some of this stems from the US embargo, but the embargo never stopped Cuba from trading with the rest of the world; the deeper problem is a centrally planned economy that has failed for 65 years to produce basic prosperity.

**Yes.** Judged by material welfare, personal freedom, and the choices Cubans have made with their own feet, most Cubans ended up worse off under the revolution than they plausibly would have been otherwise — and in many respects worse off in absolute terms.

**The economic record is damning.** In the 1950s, Cuba was one of Latin America's most advanced countries — high calorie consumption, one of the region's higher incomes per person, and by some economic historians' estimates living standards comparable to Southern Europe, albeit with severe rural poverty and inequality. Today Cuba trails Costa Rica, Chile, Panama, and the Dominican Republic — countries it once led. The revolution abolished private farming and most private enterprise, and productivity collapsed: a nation that was the world's dominant sugar exporter now produces roughly a tenth of its pre-revolutionary sugar. Living standards for decades depended on Soviet subsidies of several billion dollars a year; when they vanished in 1991, the economy shrank by about a third and caloric intake fell enough to cause epidemic malnutrition-related illness. Food has been rationed continuously since 1962 — a system designed as temporary that has now lasted over sixty years. The current crisis is the worst since the revolution: blackouts of ten to twenty hours, medicine shortages so severe that hospitals ask patients to bring their own sheets and syringes, and state wages of roughly $20–40 a month.

**The political record is worse still.** Cuba has held no free national election since before 1959. There is no free press, dissent is criminalized, and hundreds of people remain jailed for the July 11, 2021 protests. For most of the revolution's life, Cubans could not start a business, sell their own home (legalized only in 2011), travel abroad without state permission (until 2013), or even stay in tourist hotels. Whether or not one values these liberties as much as a full stomach, they are part of what makes a life good — and they were destroyed for everyone.

**The strongest evidence is what Cubans do when given any exit.** Roughly one in five Cubans lives abroad — one of the largest diaspora shares on earth. Hundreds of thousands have crossed ninety miles of open ocean on rafts. Nearly a tenth of the current population has left in just the last few years. People do not risk death to flee a system that made their lives better. Notably, the 2021 protests were loudest in poor, largely Afro-Cuban neighborhoods — the very constituencies the revolution claims to have lifted up.

**The fair counterargument deserves acknowledgment, but it doesn't reverse the verdict.** The revolution did achieve real things: literacy rose from roughly 75% (far lower in the countryside) to near-universal, life expectancy rose from about 60 to near 79, infant mortality plummeted, and the rural poor gained land, clinics, and schools they had been denied under Batista's dictatorship. These gains are genuine and shouldn't be denied. But three facts blunt their force. First, virtually every Latin American country achieved similar gains in literacy and mortality over the same decades without revolution — Costa Rica matched Cuba's health statistics with a democracy and a mixed economy. Second, Cuba's gains were subsidized by Soviet oil and hard-currency exports of doctors, and the system proved incapable of sustaining them: today a Cuban mother cannot reliably find children's aspirin. Third, even granting the gains, "most Cubans" must be judged on the whole bundle of life — food, housing, opportunity, freedom, hope — and on that bundle, the urban middle class lost everything, the rural poor gained literacy while trading chronic scarcity for political subjection, and by the 1990s and again today, material deprivation has spread to nearly everyone.

Yes, the U.S. embargo imposed real costs, and it's fair to note it. But Cuba could always trade with Europe, Latin America, and Asia; the deeper cause of stagnation is the domestic model itself — command economies without private property failed everywhere they were tried, and the ones that liberalized (China, Vietnam) prospered.

So the verdict stands: for most Cubans, the revolution made life worse — poorer, less free, and with less future, which is precisely why so many of them keep leaving.

People do not flee a country en masse, year after year, on rafts where thousands have drowned, because life is better. The economic case is strong too. Most economists find that immigration raises overall growth and has little effect on average native wages. Immigrants are disproportionately represented among startup founders, patent holders, and workers in both high-skill and essential lower-wage sectors. The fiscal effects also run positive: the CBO projected that recent elevated immigration would reduce federal deficits by roughly $900 billion over a decade through added labor force participation and tax revenue.

The strongest counterarguments are real but don't flip the conclusion. The least-educated native workers may face modest wage pressure, but that's better addressed through training, wage subsidies, and labor standards enforcement than by forfeiting immigration's larger gains. Concerns about absorption—housing, infrastructure—are better solved by building more housing and infrastructure than by keeping people out. And objections rooted purely in cultural preference are values rather than evidence—and on that terrain, America's own history as a nation of immigrants cuts the other way.

One nuance: "increase" should mean expanded legal channels, especially employment- and skills-based ones, with orderly processing and enforcement targeted at genuine security risks rather than migration itself. But the direction is clear—more, not less.
